chunk_findings.detail:
`ItemEdit.queue` is only forwarded on the non-worktree path:

```python
    if edit.worktree is not None:
        return _update_and_rebind(repo, log, cfg, item, fields, edit.worktree)   # no queue
    return _record_update(log, cfg, it, fields, queue=edit.queue)
```

`_update_and_rebind` receives only `fields` (and the worktree path), never `edit.queue`, and it is the only other place a glob/resource re-target happens. So given the input `ddflow update --item X --globs help.py --queue --worktree WT`, the code takes the early return at line 84, `_waiting(...)` (the sole caller of `WG.register`/`WG.release_advice`) is never reached, no `waiting_on` record is registered for the requested glob, and the cycle/release advice machinery never fires for this update. Two agents each widening onto a glob the other holds will therefore both keep their old leases and poll forever — the exact hold-and-wait deadlock this change exists to remove — silently, because `--queue` is accepted by the model but has no effect on this path. Same for `claim` if it routes through this entry point.

chunk_findings.detail: A claim refused because a queued waiter is ahead (`_refuse_if_queued` returning `O.refused(..., queued_behind=...)`) never calls `_record_waiting`; the only registration site is the `except` branch in `_acquire` around the `L.acquire` live-holder refusal. So waiters that are merely *behind the queue* get no `waiting_on` record: no `since`, no participation in `WG`'s cycle detection, and no `[lease].wait_max_s` release. Concrete failure: C claims `h.py` (held by A) and is recorded waiting for it. B then claims `h.py` with `--queue`; it is refused "queued behind C" and is *not* recorded. Meanwhile A claims `g1` (held by B), is refused by `L.acquire`, and is recorded waiting for B. The cycle A→B→A now exists, but on A's registration the second refusal cannot see B because B has no record, so `DX-lease-wait-cycle` detection never fires and the pair sits in hold-and-wait. The regression test ("two items that each want a glob the other holds are detected on the second refusal") only passes as long as neither party was ever told it was queued behind a third party; add a third waiter and detection silently stops working.

chunk_findings.detail: The queue-ahead check is skipped whenever the item already held a lease (`held_before`) or `force` is set — i.e. exactly the widening case the change is about. A widening claim therefore bypasses FIFO and can take a glob a waiter queued for. Concrete failure: agent W queues for `g.py`, which item Z holds, so W is recorded waiting for `g.py` (since t0). When Z releases `g.py`, item X — which already holds its own lease `h.py` and is now widening to `g.py` — calls claim with `want=[g.py]`; `held_before` is true, so `_refuse_if_queued` returns `None`, `L.acquire` finds no live holder and succeeds, and X takes `g.py` even though W is ahead in the queue. W's next attempt is refused again, so the waiter is starved and the hold-and-wait the change aims to break is re-introduced for holders. (The same `skip` makes `force`/update widening bypass the queue entirely.)

chunk_findings.detail:
The change binds `waits` in exactly one place — `waits = WG.rows(st, cfg, time.time())` added at new lines 198–201, inside the function that builds the `data` mapping (`data["contested"] = contested`, `data["waiting"] = waits`, `data["taken_over"] = [{"id": ..., "holder": ..., "taken_over_by": ...}]`). chunk_findings.detail: The new verbatim whitelist registers `holder`, `lease_event` and `on` for `lease.waiting`, but not the fields that carry the waiter's own request: `globs` (and the agent ids inside `queue`). The same change's own comment in `ddflow/core/records.py` declares the record as `{"holder", "globs", "on", "since", "queue", "ttl_s", "lease_event", "agent", "at"}`, and the author protected the sibling values for exactly this reason — `holder` is annotated "an agent id compared with a lease's holder" and `on` is annotated "…glob pairs of the leases waited for", i.e. agent ids and glob values are values the redactor rewrites when the event is written to the log. chunk_findings.detail: The `lines += [...]` statement is indented inside the outer `for ln in lanes:` body (8 spaces, same level as the `if`), and its comprehension iterates `for ln in lanes` again — all lanes, for every lane. The result is that every wait line is emitted once per active lane instead of once. Concretely, with two active lanes A and B where A has a standing wait record, `build()`/render produces the outer loop twice and each pass re-scans both lanes, so A's wait line appears twice in the printed output; with N lanes it appears N times, and the listing's size grows as O(lanes × waits) rather than O(waits). The fix is to dedent the line out of the outer loop (or iterate only over the current `ln.waits`), since the comprehension already performs the full traversal itself.

chunk_findings.detail:
`edges()` now deliberately returns two *kinds* of dependency (a `["queue", ""]` edge for the waiter ahead, distinct from the hold edges `blockers()` produces), but `register()` still decides "nothing changed" by comparing only the `item` names of `prior["on"]` and `on`. When an item switches role for the same waiter, the two lists have identical `item` names and the function returns the stale prior row instead of appending the new edges, so the returned record (and the row it represents) keeps a holder/pair that is no longer true and never records the queue edge.

Concrete input that reaches it:

- Waiter W asks for globs `[g1, g2]`.
- Agent `AA` holds `g1`; agent `ZZ` holds `g2` and is (already) queued ahead of W for `g1`.
- First `register`: `blockers` = `[(AA,g1),(ZZ,g2)]`, and the queue-ahead `ZZ` is suppressed by the `all(o["item"] != ahead.item ...)` guard, so `on` items are `[AA, ZZ]`, both hold edges (`prior["on"]`).
- `ZZ` now releases `g2` but keeps waiting for `g1`.
- Second `register` (within `_refresh_s`, which is the normal case for a polling agent): `blockers` = `[(AA,g1)]`, `queue_ahead` = `ZZ`, so `edges` = `[AA (hold g1), ZZ (queue)]` — `item` names `[AA, ZZ]`, equal to `prior["on"]`.
- Because `same`, `prior["queue"] == queue`, and the item lists match, `register` returns `prior` without appending, even though `ZZ` no longer holds `g2` and the edge is now a queue dependency.

Result: the record handed back to the caller and kept in the log still reports `ZZ` as holding `g2` (stale `holder`/`pair`) and omits the queue relationship to `ZZ`; anything that names the glob/agent to release from this record acts on information that is no longer true. The comparison needs to include the edge kind (`pair`), not just the item id.

chunk_findings.detail: `_refuse_if_queued` is the change's FIFO gate for the free-glob handoff (it is the only place that refuses a claim whose wanted glob is currently **free** but already claimed in the queue by an earlier waiter; `L.acquire` only sees current holders). It is skipped whenever `held_before` is true, and `held_before` is true precisely for `ddflow update --globs` widening — the case the whole change exists to serialize. Concrete failure: B holds glob `g2`; A holds `g1` and runs `ddflow update --globs g1,g2 --queue`, is refused, and is recorded waiting for `g2` by `_record_waiting`. B releases `g2`. Before A re-acquires, C holds `g3` and runs `ddflow update --globs g3,g2 --queue`: because C already holds a lease, `held_before=True`, so `_refuse_if_queued` returns `None` and the claim proceeds to `L.acquire`, which hands the now-free `g2` to C. A is starved until `[lease].wait_max_s`, violating the stated requirement "FIFO per glob so a waiter is not starved" and re-introducing the leapfrog the change was meant to prevent. The skip is only valid for a pure refresh (wanted globs are already all held); it must not apply when the claim adds new globs that an earlier waiter has queued for.

chunk_findings.detail: The refusal text was rewritten to assert, unconditionally, that the request "is recorded as waiting" and to instruct the agent "Do not poll." Per the stated design, the `waiting_on` record is only registered when the caller opts in with `--queue` (`ddflow update --globs` / `ddflow claim` take an *optional* `--queue`; without it the refusal is immediate and nothing is queued). This hunk has no branch on the queue flag: every collision — including a plain `ddflow update --globs` with no `--queue` — returns the new message. Input: agent A holds `help.py`; agent B runs `ddflow update --globs 'help.py'` without `--queue`. B gets back "the globs were not changed; your lease stays as it is and the request is recorded as waiting. Do not poll …", but no `lease.waiting` record was written, so `WG.rows`/`_with_waits` will never show B as a waiter and the cycle-detection/progress-break machinery described in the intent will never fire for B. B has been told to stop polling on the basis of a record that does not exist, so it waits indefinitely (or must ignore the instruction), which is exactly the stall the change is meant to remove. The `if globs is not None:` FIFO check below is likewise reached without consulting any queue flag, so even a non-queueing caller can now be refused because someone else is ahead in a queue it never joined. The message needs to be conditioned on whether a `waiting_on` record was actually created (and the queue-ahead check gated the same way), or it becomes a false promise to the agent.

chunk_findings.detail:
The FIFO comparison uses the *existing record's* `since` as the requester's place, but `register` re-starts `since` at `now` whenever the request is not identical (`same` is false when `sorted(prior["globs"]) != sorted(globs)`). So the decision and the row that is stored disagree for a changed request, and a later request can jump a queued waiter.

Concrete input: agent/item A has a standing wait recorded at `since=T0` for globs `["x.txt"]` (blocked by D). Agent/item W, queued (`--queue`), has been standing since `since=T1 > T0` for globs `["*.py"]` (blocked by C). At `T2`, A calls `update --globs x.txt,help.py`; `blockers(A)` is empty (nothing holds `help.py`), `queue_ahead(A, globs=["help.py"])` finds W, overlaps `["*.py"]`→`["help.py"]`, but skips it because `w["since"] (T1) >= cutoff (T0)`, so it returns `None`; `edges()` therefore yields no edge and `register` returns `None`, i.e. A's request is *granted* even though W asked for overlapping files first (`T1 < T2`). `register` then stores A's record with `since=T2` anyway — so the same call both decides with the old position and records the new one. This contradicts the module's own rule ("a later request for files an earlier queued waiter asked for is refused as queued behind it") and requirement (3) "FIFO per glob so a waiter is not starved": W, which asked first for the glob, is pushed behind a requester that only asked for it at T2. The requester's place must be the `since` it is about to be recorded with (i.e. `now` when `same` is false), not the stale record's.

chunk_findings.detail: Both new `queue` parameters advertise a config-backed default — claim's help says "Either way the refusal is recorded as waiting and returns at once ([lease].wait_queue makes it the default)" and update's says "keep the request in the first-in-first-out line for them ([lease].wait_queue makes it the default)". Nothing in the reviewed change ever consumes `wait_queue`: the `Param("queue", type="boolean", help=..., cli_help=...)` declarations declare no `default` (contrast the neighbouring `resources` Param, which ends with `default=""`), and the handler side hard-codes `queue=bool(a.get("queue"))`. With a project config containing `[lease].wait_queue = true`, a call such as `ddflow claim ID --globs help.py` (or `ddflow update ID --globs help.py`) made while another lease holds `help.py` still evaluates `a.get("queue")` to `None` → `bool(None) == False`, so the agent is refused and *not* placed in the per-glob FIFO line, exactly the hold-and-wait situation the change is meant to remove. The documented file-level knob is therefore dead: the default queueing promised by the help text never happens, and the "defaults overridable per project and org" requirement stated in the change's own conformance note ([r-everything-configurable] / D-universal-principles) is not met by this part of the change. This is only demonstrable if no other part of the 11-part change wires `lease.wait_queue` into the parameter resolver before the handler runs; based on the code shown here, it is not wired.

chunk_findings.detail: The call being asserted on (context line 156, `run_cli(repo, "update", "T1", "--globs", "src/a.py,docs/x.md", agent=HOLDER)`) passes no `--queue`, yet the new assertion requires exactly one `lease.waiting` event to be appended. This test therefore has exactly two possible readings, and both are defects. (a) If the implementation honours the opt-in, a plain refusal records nothing — the assertion this diff *deletes* (`len(...) == n`) was the correct one — so the displayed line fails deterministically on every run against `update --globs` without `--queue`. (b) If the implementation actually appends `lease.waiting` on every refusal, the test passes but encodes behavior that contradicts item (1) of the intent: an agent that never asked to wait (e.g. one stuck in exactly the polling loop this change is meant to eliminate) is silently enrolled as a waiter. That enrollment has observable consequences under the rest of the spec — the record "expires with the waiter's lease", it participates in "FIFO per glob", and per item (2) a waiter that cannot get the globs within `[lease].wait_max_s` gets told to release the globs other agents want. So an agent that merely retried a failing `update --globs` can be named by the scheduler and told to drop its current lease (e.g. the hot help.py) without ever requesting queueing, and it occupies a FIFO slot ahead of agents that did pass `--queue`. `ItemEdit.queue` is only forwarded on the non-worktree path:

```python
    if edit.worktree is not None:
        return _update_and_rebind(repo, log, cfg, item, fields, edit.worktree)   # no queue
    return _record_update(log, cfg, it, fields, queue=edit.queue)

chunk_findings.detail: A claim refused because a queued waiter is ahead (`_refuse_if_queued` returning `O.refused(..., queued_behind=...)`) never calls `_record_waiting`; the only registration site is the `except` branch in `_acquire` around the `L.acquire` live-holder refusal. So waiters that are merely *behind the queue* get no `waiting_on` record: no `since`, no participation in `WG`'s cycle detection, and no `[lease].wait_max_s` release. Concrete failure: C claims `h.py` (held by A) and is recorded waiting for it. B then claims `h.py` with `--queue`; it is refused "queued behind C" and is *not* recorded. Meanwhile A claims `g1` (held by B), is refused by `L.acquire`, and is recorded waiting for B. The cycle A→B→A now exists, but on A's registration the second refusal cannot see B because B has no record, so `DX-lease-wait-cycle` detection never fires and the pair sits in hold-and-wait. The regression test ("two items that each want a glob the other holds are detected on the second refusal") only passes as long as neither party was ever told it was queued behind a third party; add a third waiter and detection silently stops working.

chunk_findings.detail: The new verbatim whitelist registers `holder`, `lease_event` and `on` for `lease.waiting`, but not the fields that carry the waiter's own request: `globs` (and the agent ids inside `queue`). The same change's own comment in `ddflow/core/records.py` declares the record as `{"holder", "globs", "on", "since", "queue", "ttl_s", "lease_event", "agent", "at"}`, and the author protected the sibling values for exactly this reason — `holder` is annotated "an agent id compared with a lease's holder" and `on` is annotated "…glob pairs of the leases waited for", i.e. agent ids and glob values are values the redactor rewrites when the event is written to the log. chunk_findings.detail:
`edges()` now deliberately returns two *kinds* of dependency (a `["queue", ""]` edge for the waiter ahead, distinct from the hold edges `blockers()` produces), but `register()` still decides "nothing changed" by comparing only the `item` names of `prior["on"]` and `on`. When an item switches role for the same waiter, the two lists have identical `item` names and the function returns the stale prior row instead of appending the new edges, so the returned record (and the row it represents) keeps a holder/pair that is no longer true and never records the queue edge.

Concrete input that reaches it:

- Waiter W asks for globs `[g1, g2]`.
- Agent `AA` holds `g1`; agent `ZZ` holds `g2` and is (already) queued ahead of W for `g1`.
- First `register`: `blockers` = `[(AA,g1),(ZZ,g2)]`, and the queue-ahead `ZZ` is suppressed by the `all(o["item"] != ahead.item ...)` guard, so `on` items are `[AA, ZZ]`, both hold edges (`prior["on"]`).
- `ZZ` now releases `g2` but keeps waiting for `g1`.
- Second `register` (within `_refresh_s`, which is the normal case for a polling agent): `blockers` = `[(AA,g1)]`, `queue_ahead` = `ZZ`, so `edges` = `[AA (hold g1), ZZ (queue)]` — `item` names `[AA, ZZ]`, equal to `prior["on"]`.
- Because `same`, `prior["queue"] == queue`, and the item lists match, `register` returns `prior` without appending, even though `ZZ` no longer holds `g2` and the edge is now a queue dependency.

Result: the record handed back to the caller and kept in the log still reports `ZZ` as holding `g2` (stale `holder`/`pair`) and omits the queue relationship to `ZZ`; anything that names the glob/agent to release from this record acts on information that is no longer true. The comparison needs to include the edge kind (`pair`), not just the item id.

chunk_findings.detail: `_refuse_if_queued` is the change's FIFO gate for the free-glob handoff (it is the only place that refuses a claim whose wanted glob is currently **free** but already claimed in the queue by an earlier waiter; `L.acquire` only sees current holders). It is skipped whenever `held_before` is true, and `held_before` is true precisely for `ddflow update --globs` widening — the case the whole change exists to serialize. Concrete failure: B holds glob `g2`; A holds `g1` and runs `ddflow update --globs g1,g2 --queue`, is refused, and is recorded waiting for `g2` by `_record_waiting`. B releases `g2`. Before A re-acquires, C holds `g3` and runs `ddflow update --globs g3,g2 --queue`: because C already holds a lease, `held_before=True`, so `_refuse_if_queued` returns `None` and the claim proceeds to `L.acquire`, which hands the now-free `g2` to C. A is starved until `[lease].wait_max_s`, violating the stated requirement "FIFO per glob so a waiter is not starved" and re-introducing the leapfrog the change was meant to prevent. The skip is only valid for a pure refresh (wanted globs are already all held); it must not apply when the claim adds new globs that an earlier waiter has queued for.

chunk_findings.detail: The refusal text was rewritten to assert, unconditionally, that the request "is recorded as waiting" and to instruct the agent "Do not poll." Per the stated design, the `waiting_on` record is only registered when the caller opts in with `--queue` (`ddflow update --globs` / `ddflow claim` take an *optional* `--queue`; without it the refusal is immediate and nothing is queued). This hunk has no branch on the queue flag: every collision — including a plain `ddflow update --globs` with no `--queue` — returns the new message. Input: agent A holds `help.py`; agent B runs `ddflow update --globs 'help.py'` without `--queue`. B gets back "the globs were not changed; your lease stays as it is and the request is recorded as waiting. Do not poll …", but no `lease.waiting` record was written, so `WG.rows`/`_with_waits` will never show B as a waiter and the cycle-detection/progress-break machinery described in the intent will never fire for B. B has been told to stop polling on the basis of a record that does not exist, so it waits indefinitely (or must ignore the instruction), which is exactly the stall the change is meant to remove. The `if globs is not None:` FIFO check below is likewise reached without consulting any queue flag, so even a non-queueing caller can now be refused because someone else is ahead in a queue it never joined. The message needs to be conditioned on whether a `waiting_on` record was actually created (and the queue-ahead check gated the same way), or it becomes a false promise to the agent.

chunk_findings.detail:
The FIFO comparison uses the *existing record's* `since` as the requester's place, but `register` re-starts `since` at `now` whenever the request is not identical (`same` is false when `sorted(prior["globs"]) != sorted(globs)`). So the decision and the row that is stored disagree for a changed request, and a later request can jump a queued waiter.

Concrete input: agent/item A has a standing wait recorded at `since=T0` for globs `["x.txt"]` (blocked by D). Agent/item W, queued (`--queue`), has been standing since `since=T1 > T0` for globs `["*.py"]` (blocked by C). At `T2`, A calls `update --globs x.txt,help.py`; `blockers(A)` is empty (nothing holds `help.py`), `queue_ahead(A, globs=["help.py"])` finds W, overlaps `["*.py"]`→`["help.py"]`, but skips it because `w["since"] (T1) >= cutoff (T0)`, so it returns `None`; `edges()` therefore yields no edge and `register` returns `None`, i.e. A's request is *granted* even though W asked for overlapping files first (`T1 < T2`). `register` then stores A's record with `since=T2` anyway — so the same call both decides with the old position and records the new one. This contradicts the module's own rule ("a later request for files an earlier queued waiter asked for is refused as queued behind it") and requirement (3) "FIFO per glob so a waiter is not starved": W, which asked first for the glob, is pushed behind a requester that only asked for it at T2. The requester's place must be the `since` it is about to be recorded with (i.e. `now` when `same` is false), not the stale record's.

chunk_findings.detail: Both new `queue` parameters advertise a config-backed default — claim's help says "Either way the refusal is recorded as waiting and returns at once ([lease].wait_queue makes it the default)" and update's says "keep the request in the first-in-first-out line for them ([lease].wait_queue makes it the default)". With a project config containing `[lease].wait_queue = true`, a call such as `ddflow claim ID --globs help.py` (or `ddflow update ID --globs help.py`) made while another lease holds `help.py` still evaluates `a.get("queue")` to `None` → `bool(None) == False`, so the agent is refused and *not* placed in the per-glob FIFO line, exactly the hold-and-wait situation the change is meant to remove. The documented file-level knob is therefore dead: the default queueing promised by the help text never happens, and the "defaults overridable per project and org" requirement stated in the change's own conformance note ([r-everything-configurable] / D-universal-principles) is not met by this part of the change. chunk_findings.detail: The call being asserted on (context line 156, `run_cli(repo, "update", "T1", "--globs", "src/a.py,docs/x.md", agent=HOLDER)`) passes no `--queue`, yet the new assertion requires exactly one `lease.waiting` event to be appended. Per the change's own spec, the waiting record is an opt-in: "`ddflow update --globs` and `ddflow claim` take an optional `--queue`: the refusal registers a waiting_on record (who, which globs, since when)". This test therefore has exactly two possible readings, and both are defects. (a) If the implementation honours the opt-in, a plain refusal records nothing — the assertion this diff *deletes* (`len(...) == n`) was the correct one — so the displayed line fails deterministically on every run against `update --globs` without `--queue`. (b) If the implementation actually appends `lease.waiting` on every refusal, the test passes but encodes behavior that contradicts item (1) of the intent: an agent that never asked to wait (e.g. one stuck in exactly the polling loop this change is meant to eliminate) is silently enrolled as a waiter. That enrollment has observable consequences under the rest of the spec — the record "expires with the waiter's lease", it participates in "FIFO per glob", and per item (2) a waiter that cannot get the globs within `[lease].wait_max_s` gets told to release the globs other agents want. So an agent that merely retried a failing `update --globs` can be named by the scheduler and told to drop its current lease (e.g. the hot help.py) without ever requesting queueing, and it occupies a FIFO slot ahead of agents that did pass `--queue`. The test should either pass `--queue` explicitly, or assert that a non-`--queue` refusal records no `lease.waiting` event; as written it cannot distinguish correct from incorrect behavior.

chunk_findings.detail:
The test claims to prove that changing a request moves the waiter to the back of the line, but its assertion cannot observe that behavior. After setup, the queue for `src/b.py` contains exactly two entities: `T1` (queued first) and `T3` (queued second, refused behind `T1`). The final check

    WG.queue_ahead(st, cfg, "T3", "agent-c", ["src/b.py", "x.md"], time.time()).item == "T1"

is true both when `T3` keeps its original queue position and when it is re-queued at the new ask's time, because `T1` was enqueued strictly earlier in either interpretation and there is no third waiter whose relative order could flip. So an implementation that ignores changed requests entirely (the exact defect the test is named for, which would let `T3` keep priority over any later waiter and reintroduce hold-and-wait starvation) still passes. To make the assertion meaningful, the test needs a second waiter that queues between `T1` and `T3` (or must compare the stored `waiting["T3"]["at"]`/`since` values before and after the change), so that the two interpretations produce different `ahead` results. As written the comment "its place is the new ask's, not the old" is not verified by anything in the test.

(a) If the implementation honours the opt-in, a plain refusal records nothing — the assertion this diff *deletes* (`len(...) == n`) was the correct one — so the displayed line fails deterministically on every run against `update --globs` without `--queue`. (b) If the implementation actually appends `lease.waiting` on every refusal, the test passes but encodes behavior that contradicts item (1) of the intent: an agent that never asked to wait (e.g. one stuck in exactly the polling loop this change is meant to eliminate) is silently enrolled as a waiter. That enrollment has observable consequences under the rest of the spec — the record "expires with the waiter's lease", it participates in "FIFO per glob", and per item (2) a waiter that cannot get the globs within `[lease].wait_max_s` gets told to release the globs other agents want. So an agent that merely retried a failing `update --globs` can be named by the scheduler and told to drop its current lease (e.g. the hot help.py) without ever requesting queueing, and it occupies a FIFO slot ahead of agents that did pass `--queue`. The test should either pass `--queue` explicitly, or assert that a non-`--queue` refusal records no `lease.waiting` event; as written it cannot distinguish correct from incorrect behavior.

chunk_findings.detail:
The test claims to prove that changing a request moves the waiter to the back of the line, but its assertion cannot observe that behavior. After setup, the queue for `src/b.py` contains exactly two entities: `T1` (queued first) and `T3` (queued second, refused behind `T1`). The final check

    WG.queue_ahead(st, cfg, "T3", "agent-c", ["src/b.py", "x.md"], time.time()).item == "T1"

is true both when `T3` keeps its original queue position and when it is re-queued at the new ask's time, because `T1` was enqueued strictly earlier in either interpretation and there is no third waiter whose relative order could flip. So an implementation that ignores changed requests entirely (the exact defect the test is named for, which would let `T3` keep priority over any later waiter and reintroduce hold-and-wait starvation) still passes. To make the assertion meaningful, the test needs a second waiter that queues between `T1` and `T3` (or must compare the stored `waiting["T3"]["at"]`/`since` values before and after the change), so that the two interpretations produce different `ahead` results. As written the comment "its place is the new ask's, not the old" is not verified by anything in the test.
